# Stage 2.1: Additional Explorations of Data

## About
These next four questions start looking at geographic aspect of CMS and how this is interconnected with racial breakdowns, suspension rates, and reported crime.

### Dataset
For these next four questions I used a few new datasets. They include: cms_school_locations.csv which gives the geographic location of every CMS school, pupils_in_membership_by_race_and_sex_24-25.csv which gives the race and sex breakdown of each CMS school, and finally Violent_Crime_Data.geojson which is a list of reported crime throughout the Charlotte/Mecklenburg county area.

### Research Question
This information is the same is stage2.qmd

## Loading and Merging Initial Datasets

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from pyprojroot import here

race_enrollment = pd.read_csv(here("projects/hayden_project/datasets_files/pupils_in_membership_by_race_and_sex_24-25.csv"))

print(race_enrollment.shape)
print(race_enrollment.head())
print(race_enrollment.columns.tolist())
```

There's some cleaning that I need to do convert certain comma sperated values to numbers and making sure that values in two different datasets are able to be merged so I'm going to do that quickly. 

```{python}
race_enrollment = race_enrollment.copy()

race_enrollment['School'] = race_enrollment['School'].astype(str)

race_enrollment['Total'] = (race_enrollment['Total'].astype(str).str.replace(',', '', regex = False).astype(int))
```

OK this looks good yay!! Now merge and create matching school codes

```{python}
meck_all = pd.read_csv(
    here("projects/hayden_project/datasets_files/meck_all.csv"))

cms = meck_all[meck_all['agency_code'].astype(str).str.startswith('600')].copy()

print(cms.shape)
print(cms[['agency_code', 'name']].head())

cms['School'] = cms['agency_code'].astype(str).str[-3:]

cms_race = cms.merge(
    race_enrollment,
    on = 'School',
    how = 'left',
    suffixes = ('_discipline', 'enrollment'))

cms_race.head(10)

print(cms[['agency_code', 'School', 'name']].head())
```

Ok merge complete. Everything matched up nciely. meck_all is from stage2.qmd it includes disciplinary data. 

## Question 1: How does racial composition vary across Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools (CMS)?

Building off the analysis that I did in my stage2.qmd, I finally found a dataset that includes the racial breakdown of all of CMS. I'm going to start by looking at schools with the highest and lowest percentage of different races and move from there. As of right now I'm not planning to look at sex so I'm going to combine the male and female counts for each racial group.

```{python}
cms_race['pct_black'] = (
    (cms_race['BLACK Male'] + cms_race['BLACK Female'])/
    cms_race['Total'] * 100)

cms_race['pct_white'] = (
    (cms_race['WHITE Male'] + cms_race['WHITE Female'])/
    cms_race['Total'] * 100) 

cms_race['pct_hispanic'] = (
    (cms_race['HISPANIC Male'] + cms_race['HISPANIC Female'])/
    cms_race['Total'] * 100)
```

```{python}
print("Median percentage of Black students:", cms_race['pct_black'].median())

print("Lowest percentage of Black students:", cms_race['pct_black'].min())

print("Highest percentage of Black students:", cms_race['pct_black'].max())

print(cms_race[['name', 'pct_black', 'sts_per1000', 'iss_per1000']].sort_values('pct_black').head(10))

print(cms_race[['name', 'pct_black', 'sts_per1000', 'iss_per1000']].sort_values('pct_black', ascending = False).head(10))

```

When looking at these outputs we see substantial variation in racial compostion across CMS. The median percentage of Black students across CMS was roughly 34% however this percentage ranged from 0% to 80.1%. I included the STS and ISS values for the top 10 and bottom 10 schools and noticed that generally speaking schools with higher percentages of Black students also had higher suspension rates. However, this pattern wasn't always the case suggesting there are likely other outside factors. These findings are pretty similar to a question I asked previoulsy but I thought it was important to take a look at since I'm using a different dataset now. 

## Question 2: Where are CMS schools located with different demographic and disciplanry breakdowns located?

Ok I now want to move onto looking at the geographic aspect of this analysis a bit more. I thought a good intro to this would be to look at the location of schools. The dataset I'm using already has school adresses, cities, and zip codes but not lat and long values so I'm going to have to first find those which with a little research I learned I can do by using geopy.

```{python}
from geopy.geocoders import Nominatim
from geopy.extra.rate_limiter import RateLimiter

geolocator = Nominatim(user_agent = "cms_school_geo")

geocode = RateLimiter(geolocator.geocode, min_delay_seconds = 1.1, max_retries = 2)

school_locations = cms[['agency_code', 'name', 'street_addr', 'city', 'state', 'zip']].copy()

school_locations['full_address'] = (school_locations['street_addr'].astype(str) + ', ' + school_locations['city'].astype(str) + ', ' + school_locations['state'].astype(str) + ', ' + school_locations['zip'].astype(str).str.replace(r'\.0$', '', regex = True) + ', USA')

school_locations['location'] = school_locations['full_address'].apply(geocode)

school_locations['latitude'] = school_locations['location'].apply(lambda loc: loc.latitude if loc else None)

school_locations['longitude'] = school_locations['location'].apply(lambda loc: loc.longitude if loc else None)

school_locations.to_csv(here("projects/hayden_project/datasets_files/cms_school_locations.csv"), index=False)
```

Ok that took like way way longer than I was expecting, but I think it's kinda crucial to my project so hopefully that's the last of that. We now have lat and long values for 180/186 of the schools so we can look at some geography stuff. I will probably try and fill in the missing 6 schools by hand. 

I now need to do another merge so that I can have one data frame that has coordinates, racial breakdown, and suspension rates info.

```{python}
school_coords = school_locations[['agency_code', 'latitude', 'longitude']].copy()

cms_map_info = cms_race.merge(school_coords, on = 'agency_code', how = 'left')

```

PLOT TIME!! I'm using plotly also via help of StackOverflow. This plot is going to map the location of each individual school and then the color will be based on the percent of students that are black and it will also include the STS and ISS levels of that school through the hover feature. 

Also FYI you may have to zoom out a lot and then zoom back in on Mecklenburg county to view it, couldn't figure out how to set where it auto zooms to.

```{python}
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter_map(
    cms_map_info,
    lat = 'latitude',
    lon = 'longitude',
    color = 'pct_black',
    hover_name = 'name',
    hover_data = {
        'pct_black': ':.1f',
        'sts_per1000': ':.1f',
        'iss_per1000': ':.1f',
        'latitude': False,
        'longitude': False},
    color_continuous_scale = 'Viridis',
    zoom = 9,
    title = 'Racial Composition of Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools')

fig.show()
```

This looks far from random!!!! When looking at the map a pretty apparent pattern becomes clear. It looks like schools with a lower percent of black students are located in the southern part of the county while higher percent schools are more northern and located in a somewhat cone-ish looking shape. This leads me to my next quesiton of why this may be? It also leaves me wondering how this relates to the demographics of surrounding areas and neighborhoods relative to schools. 

I'm kinda needing a lot of datasets at this point, but I guess it's better to explore too many than too few. The next thing I'm going to look at I think is the racial dispersion of Mecklenburg county as a whole.

Looking at neighborhood demographics is scaring me a bit so I'm going to pivot a bit and look at the criminal activity throughout Mecklenburg county. 

## Question 3: What type of reported crime is the most common in the Charlotte/Mecklenburg County area?

Ok lets look at a dataset from the CMPD that is a record of violent crime in the area.

```{python}
import geopandas as gpd

crime = gpd.read_file(here(
    "projects/hayden_project/datasets_files/Violent_Crime_Data.geojson"))

print(crime.shape)
print(crime.crs)
print(crime.columns.tolist())
print(crime.head())
```

Let's look at some patterns over time.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

overall_crime = crime[
    (crime['ROW_TYPE'] == 'CMPD Jurisdiction') &
    (crime['OFFENSE_DESCRIPTION'] == 'Violent Crime')].copy()

overall_crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'] = pd.to_numeric(overall_crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'])
overall_crime['OFFENSE_COUNT'] = pd.to_numeric(overall_crime['OFFENSE_COUNT'])

annual_crime = (overall_crime.groupby('CALENDAR_YEAR')['OFFENSE_COUNT'].sum().reset_index().sort_values('CALENDAR_YEAR'))

annual_crime = annual_crime[annual_crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'] < 2026]

plt.figure(figsize = (10, 5))
plt.plot(
    annual_crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'],
    annual_crime['OFFENSE_COUNT'],
    marker = 'o')

plt.title('Reported Violent Crime in Charlotte-Mecklenburg, 2015–2025')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Annual reported violent-crime count')
plt.xticks(annual_crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'], rotation=45)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(annual_crime.to_string(index=False))
```

This is an interesting pattern, I might do some history/lit exploration of the why behind this pattern.

I'm going to look at the different types of crime next.

```{python}
offense_trends = crime[
    (crime['ROW_TYPE'] == 'CMPD Jurisdiction') &
    (crime['OFFENSE_DESCRIPTION'] != 'Violent Crime')].copy()

offense_trends['CALENDAR_YEAR'] = pd.to_numeric(
    offense_trends['CALENDAR_YEAR'])
offense_trends['OFFENSE_COUNT'] = pd.to_numeric(
    offense_trends['OFFENSE_COUNT'])

annual_offenses = (
    offense_trends
    .groupby(['CALENDAR_YEAR', 'OFFENSE_DESCRIPTION'])['OFFENSE_COUNT']
    .sum()
    .reset_index())

annual_offenses = annual_offenses[
    annual_offenses['CALENDAR_YEAR'] < 2026]

print(annual_offenses.head(15))
```

This is interesting to look at. It looks like Aggravated Assault-Gun has by far the most amount of offense counts. Unforutnately this data does not give us any information about the person's age. I haven't been able to find a dataset that does this.

## Question 4: How do reported violent crime vary across Charlotte-Mecklenburg’s Neighborhood Profile Areas?

Working off of this same data I'm wanting to look at how violent crime reports differ accross NPA's. I hope to maybe define these NPAs at some point. But we'll see. I need to start narrowing down what I'm doing.

```{python}
npa_crime_2025 = crime[
    (crime['ROW_TYPE'] == 'Neighborhood Profile Area') &
    (crime['OFFENSE_DESCRIPTION'] == 'Violent Crime') &
    (crime['CALENDAR_YEAR'].astype(str) == '2025')].copy()

npa_crime_2025['OFFENSE_COUNT'] = pd.to_numeric(
    npa_crime_2025['OFFENSE_COUNT'],
    errors='coerce')

npa_totals = (
    npa_crime_2025
    .groupby('GEOGRAPHY')['OFFENSE_COUNT']
    .sum()
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={
        'GEOGRAPHY': 'npa',
        'OFFENSE_COUNT': 'violent_crime_count'}))

top_npas = npa_totals.sort_values(
    'violent_crime_count',
    ascending=False).head(10)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

plt.bar(
    top_npas['npa'].astype(str),
    top_npas['violent_crime_count'])

plt.title('Neighborhood Profile Areas with the Highest Reported Violent Crime, 2025')
plt.xlabel('Neighborhood Profile Area')
plt.ylabel('Reported violent-crime count')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This is a nice plot that shows that certain NPAs have higher reported counts of violent-crime. It would be interesting to identiy what these NPA numbers represent and the demographic within them.
